    Microsoft has an old, but new, idea for PC upgrades: Cloud PCs

    news analysis
    Nov 24, 20265 mins

    With PC prices going up, Microsoft is pitching Windows 365 as a way to extend the life of your current fleet.

    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 5:00
    Instaread

    Prohibitive prices have put many enterprises’ PC upgrades on hold, but Microsoft has another idea: upgrade to its “cloud PCs.”

    Cloud PCs are a reference to Windows 365, which delivers a familiar, full Windows 11 desktop experience from the Microsoft Cloud. It works on a wide range of existing computing devices.

    Users don’t need a full-featured laptop. They can get a full Windows experience by launching an app on a lower-end Windows PC, Mac, or tablet, or through a specialized remote-desktop device.

    With PC prices going up, Windows 365 allows you to extend the life of your current PC fleet, said Pavan Davuluri, executive vice president of Windows and Devices at Microsoft, during the opening-day keynote at the company’s Ignite conference last week.

    “You can give compute to anyone in minutes, no new hardware. As you plan this PC refresh cycle, add cloud PCs to your estate,” Davuluri said.

    At Ignite, Microsoft introduced new technologies to make Windows 365 faster and easier to use. The product itself was launched five years ago, so it isn’t new, nor is the concept of getting a full-fledged computing experience through a single app window, which has been considered promising for decades.

    Recommended for you
    • Microsoft will let Copilot act on local files on Windows PCs
      By Matthew Finnegan•5 mins

      By Anirban Ghoshal•5 mins
    • Microsoft cheat sheets: Dive into Windows, Office, and Copilot
      By Valerie Potter•17 mins

    In the ’80s, Sun Microsystems coined the slogan “The network is the computer,” with the promise that powerful Unix servers would deliver full computing experiences to remote desktops with minimal hardware. In the late 2000s, netbooks with underwhelming hardware also promised more web-based computing, but faded away. Chromebooks are now a conduit for running applications hosted on the internet.

    But cloud PCs could be more relevant now, especially with AI in the picture, Microsoft officials argued.

    Unlike on-premises PCs, cloud PCs are “elastic.” Enterprises can choose configurations to match the compute to work, such as 2 virtual CPUs and 4GB of RAM for running light productivity tools and more CPUs, more RAM, and even GPUs for AI and graphics-intensive jobs.

    Configurations with up to 32 virtual CPUs and 128GB of RAM are available, with prices ranging from $25 to $255 per user per month for small businesses, and from $28 to $765 per user per month for large enterprises. The top-level enterprise plans include GPUs for graphics-intensive workloads and cost up to $1,915/user/month.

    Recommended for you

    Microsoft also offers plans for running AI agents in Windows 365. There are going to be 1.3 billion agents working along with employees by 2028, according to an IDC projection shown on a Microsoft slide.

    With cloud PCs, IT administrators have a better grip over AI agents, Microsoft said. Admins also sidestep the burden of monitoring and patching a fleet of physical PCs.

    “Today if you’re still purchasing, troubleshooting, or patching a full PC for every hot desk, every station, and every shift, you’re giving back some of those savings you just made,” said Jose Lara Silva, a product manager at Microsoft.

    Microsoft has made its streaming technology, called DirectStream, faster. Connection reliability has also improved by 300%, said Bhavya Chopra, partner director for Windows 365 at Microsoft.

    “[Sessions] connect in seconds now in the right conditions… We have made a bunch of improvements to make sure that… once you click that connect button on your Windows app, you’re in the desktop within 10 seconds,” Chopra said.

    Microsoft and Nvidia also collaborated to optimize a chip, the RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, to encode graphics for DirectStream on cloud PCs.

    But there could be challenges. Chopra acknowledged that in many cases, printers and specialized USB devices don’t work yet, as extra drivers can’t be installed on locked-down cloud PC devices.

    Microsoft’s Windows 365 pitch at Ignite makes sense theoretically and for some segments of users, said Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research.

    Renting the Microsoft offering in the cloud lets CIOs skip hardware upgrades as memory and chip costs drive PC prices to record highs, Shah said.

    AI agents also need tight security, Shah said. Windows 365 lets IT administrators “manage everything centrally, keep corporate data off local drives, and run agents in isolated environments without buying expensive AI laptops for the whole company,” Shah said.

    But the reality is more complex, Shah said. “You still have to buy a physical device, screen, and keyboard just to connect to the cloud.”  When you add up four years of monthly Windows 365 subscriptions on top of that base hardware, “it often costs more than simply buying a standard laptop,” he said.

    “Also, if the internet goes down or suffers from bad latency, everything can come to a standstill,” Shah said.

    Running every token in the cloud can get expensive, whereas powerful on-premises hardware can run some AI workloads locally and privately, he noted.

    A limited cohort could benefit from Windows 365, such as contractors, offshore teams, M&A onboarding, and spinning up secure sandboxes for AI agents, Shah said. “As a full replacement for an entire company’s laptop fleet, though, the math still points toward a hybrid setup rather than going 100% cloud.”
